analysis.one_liner: Ends the exemption that lets short-term health insurance plans skip ACA coverage rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing, a floor vote, or a single cosponsor in the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Short-term, limited-duration health plans are cheap insurance products that do not have to follow the Affordable Care Act's rules — they can deny people with preexisting conditions, cap payouts, and skip required benefits. This bill would have removed that exemption starting April 1, 2023, requiring these plans to meet the same standards as regular individual coverage. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy individual health insurance, especially anyone with a preexisting condition, a chronic illness, or a serious medical bill that a skimpy short-term plan would refuse to cover. They would be protected from plans that look like insurance but leave major costs uncovered.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends federal health law so that short-term, limited-duration plans issued, sold, or renewed on or after April 1, 2023 are no longer exempt from the individual market requirements of the Affordable Care Act, which include coverage of preexisting conditions and essential benefits.
Currently these plans can offer limited coverage for a limited time while skipping ACA market rules, meaning customers can be sold coverage that fails when they get sick.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that sell short-term, limited-duration insurance lose their ability to market cheaper, skimpier plans that skip consumer protections. Some healthy buyers who relied on those plans to pay less would face higher premiums for full-coverage plans.

drawbacks.text: Short-term plans exist because they are cheaper; some healthy people without subsidies rely on them and would have to pay more for ACA-compliant coverage if the exemption disappeared.
The bill took effect immediately, on April 1, 2023, with no transition period, so people holding short-term plans at that time could have seen their coverage end abruptly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protects consumers from plans that can deny care for preexisting conditions and leave big bills unpaid, at the cost of ending a cheaper — but thinner — insurance option for some buyers. The tradeoff favors people who actually get sick, and it does nothing to lower the premiums that pushed some buyers toward junk plans in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in February 2023, sent to its Health Subcommittee days later, and never received any further action for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Castor introduced the bill on February 1, 2023 and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On February 10, 2023 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where no hearing or further action followed.
No other member cosponsored the bill and it never came to a vote in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Short-term, limited-duration insurance sellers kept their exemption and their market for cheap, skimpy plans; consumers with preexisting conditions remain exposed to them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Short-term plan sellers kept their exemption

for.name: Rep. Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee; no other member joined.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over health insurance law
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill dead in subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only a Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no party split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill removes the exemption these insurers rely on to sell plans that skip ACA protections like preexisting-condition coverage. Their cheap premiums depend on the coverage being thin, which is what costs consumers when they get sick.
Requiring short-term plans to meet the same rules would move buyers back into regulated coverage, adding healthier and sicker customers alike to the standard risk pool and stabilizing it.
